analysis.overview: ChatGPT leads on volume and approval, with 61,362 reviews and a 4.43-star rating, and its distinctive praise terms center on students, homework, and study, positioning it clearly as an everyday learning aid. Google Gemini matches that volume at 53,559 reviews and earns its 4.32 stars largely through mobile integration praise — image, video, live, and fast — making it the standout on-device assistant. Perplexity and Claude are the most polarizing products: both carry the widest standard deviations (1.56 and 1.62 respectively) and the lowest ratings (4.03 and 3.82), meaning reviewers are most split on these two, though Perplexity's distinctive praise around research, sources, and accuracy gives it a clear niche as a citation-forward search tool while Claude's praise concentrates entirely on coding and code. Claude's complaint terms — limit, message, usage, limits, messages — are essentially the same words as its praise terms, which tells a specific story: users value it for code work but hit usage caps and walk away frustrated by that single friction point. Microsoft Copilot sits in the middle on rating (4.33) but has the smallest review base (2,012), and its complaints around keyboard, copy, scroll, and line point to text-input and UI mechanics rather than AI quality, suggesting its adoption ceiling is currently a product interface problem rather than a model credibility problem.

products.ChatGPT: ChatGPT's clearest differentiator is its role as a study and homework companion: the distinctive positive keywords cluster tightly around academic use (students, study, homework, studies) and around the experience of having a knowledgeable personal resource (help, helps, friend, answer, life), which aligns with the effusive personal attachment visible in reviews like "CHATGPT IS MY BEST FRIEND." With 75.6% five-star ratings and a solid average of 4.43, satisfaction is broadly high, though a standard deviation of 1.19 and an 8% one-star share signal a meaningful minority of strongly dissatisfied users. The main pain points centre on answer accuracy and trustworthiness — negative keywords like wrong, answers, correct, trust, and information all point to users losing confidence when the app gives incorrect outputs — and separately, friction around the subscription model, with upgrade and plus suggesting complaints about paywalled features. Notably, answer appears in both positive and negative keyword sets, meaning the quality of responses is simultaneously ChatGPT's biggest draw and its most criticised weakness.
products.Claude: Claude is most distinctly associated with coding capability, with users specifically praising its performance on programming tasks, and it draws strong enthusiasm for its free tier and range of available models. The 58.6% five-star share confirms a substantial satisfied base, particularly among users with specific professional or technical use cases. However, usage limits are the single sharpest pain point and, notably, appear in both positive and negative distinctive keywords simultaneously — meaning the free tier attracts users who then frequently collide with message and usage caps, sometimes within a single session. The 20.2% one-star rate and high polarisation score of 1.62 standard deviations reflect a product that delivers strongly for some users while frustrating others with access restrictions around account verification, plan limits, and rate limiting on messages.
products.Google_Gemini: Google Gemini's standout identity is built around multimodal capability: image, video, live interaction, and phone/Android integration are its most distinctive positive associations, suggesting users value it as a deeply embedded mobile and visual AI assistant rather than a text-only tool. With 73.1% five-star reviews and a 4.32 average, satisfaction is broadly strong, though a 1.32 standard deviation and 10.8% one-star share reveal a meaningfully polarised user base. The sharpest tension in the data is that image, video, live, phone, and assistant appear in both positive and negative keyword sets, meaning these same multimodal features that earn praise are also the source of the most frustration — likely reflecting inconsistent performance in generation, loading, and editing rather than rejection of the features themselves. Slow loading, language issues, and photo/screen problems dominate negative feedback, pointing to reliability and latency gaps rather than conceptual complaints about what Gemini is trying to do.
products.Microsoft_Copilot: Microsoft Copilot's strongest distinction is its deep Windows integration, with "windows" and "direct" among its most distinctive positive terms, suggesting users value it as a native, well-embedded tool rather than a standalone add-on. Its 73.8% five-star rate and positive sentiment of 0.418 reflect a broadly satisfied base, with praise clustering around tone and politeness rather than raw capability, hinting users appreciate its communication style over competitors. The sharpest pain points are mechanical and interaction-level: negative keywords like "keyboard," "enter," "return," "sends," and "scroll" point to broken input behaviour, where basic actions like pressing Enter or copying text produce unintended results, creating the friction explicitly named in the example reviews. Image generation surfaces as a distinct fault line, appearing in negative reviews as a failure to correctly interpret requests, and the presence of "bing" and "boundaries" in negative keywords suggests users are frustrated by content restrictions and the product's inherited Bing constraints.
products.Perplexity: Perplexity stands out primarily as a research and search tool, with users distinctively praising its accuracy, depth, use of cited sources and references, and concise information gathering — qualities that set it apart from competing AI products. The 66.4% five-star rate and positive sentiment score of 0.382 suggest a solid base of enthusiastic users who value it as a serious research engine. However, the 17.7% one-star rate and a high polarisation score of 1.56 standard deviations point to a meaningful minority with strong grievances, centred on the subscription model, limits on free searches, and friction around file uploading — suggesting the paywall is a recurring frustration. Notably, "research" and "computer" appear in both the distinctive positive and negative keyword sets, indicating that the core research use case is both the product's main selling point and a source of disappointment when users hit functional or access barriers trying to perform it.
